implementation_notes: Modern C++ default: the entity stays an aggregate struct and the mapping is one constexpr descriptor built with make_storage/make_table/make_column, so column names, keys, defaults and converters live in a value the library turns into SQL. Nothing is added to the type - no base class, no virtual functions - and the storage object is injected wherever persistence is needed. Choose it for SQLite-backed C++17 code where a header-only dependency is acceptable; the classic hand-written mapper remains the fallback when the schema must be verified against types at compile time.
pitfalls: The descriptor is ordinary code: a wrong or duplicated column entry compiles and silently changes the SQL/schema, so review it like DDL.
Metadata and migration are separate: sync_schema can alter tables, but a mismatch between descriptor and database still surfaces at runtime, not at compile time.

variants.name: ODB pragmas compiled into a persistence layer
variants.idiom_name: ODB #pragma db object / #pragma db id / column
variants.implementation_notes: Classic C++ alternative: annotate the entity with ODB pragmas and let the ODB compiler generate the mapping, schema and query code, so the runtime library carries no metadata and the entity has no persistence members. Choose it in C++11+ codebases that already run a code-generation step and need several database backends; the cost is a build-system dependency and mapping errors that only the ODB compiler sees.
pitfalls: Pragmas are preprocessor directives invisible to the C++ type system: a wrong column name is caught by the ODB compiler or at runtime, never by the language.
Every changed header must be recompiled through the ODB compiler; stale generated code produces obscure link/runtime failures.
